metadata.title: Why Did MSTR, PLTR, NFLX Stocks Plummet To 52-Week Lows?

content.text:
-
MSTR slid more than 9% after Bitcoin's price fell sharply on Wednesday.
-
PLTR fell nearly 3% amid a broader market rout.
-
NFLX closed about 1.35% lower amid sustained pressure from mounting competitive concerns and acquisition failures.
Strategy (MSTR), Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR), and Netflix Inc. (NFLX) fell to fresh annual lows on Wednesday as investors rotated out of high-growth, momentum-driven stocks amid profit-taking and a renewed focus on AI-related chipmakers.
MSTR stock closed down more than 9%, PLTR fell nearly 3% and NFLX closed down about 1.35% lower.
Strategy Slips Deeper On Bitcoin Decline
Shares of MSTR fell to a 52-week low of $92.28, the lowest in more than two years, after Bitcoin fell sharply on Wednesday, adding to investor concerns about the company's financing strategy. Bitcoin fell below $60,000, hitting its lowest level since October 2024, weighing on crypto-heavy companies, including Strategy.
Meanwhile, on-chain analytics firm CryptoQuant urged the company to suspend further Bitcoin purchases and strengthen its cash reserves. Strategy held 847,363 Bitcoin worth roughly $53 billion as of June 21, with cash reserves of about $1.4 billion.
Shares of the company have been under pressure in recent times, clocking six consecutive sessions of declines, and are on track to post a second month in the red.
Meanwhile, Strategy director Jarrod M. Patten sold 1,500 Class A shares for about $159,120 on June 23 after exercising stock options, according to a report from Investing.com.
MSTR stock has declined about 40% so far in 2026, while retail sentiment has dropped from 'extremely bullish' to 'bullish' over the past day.
Palantir Drops Amid Broader Market Rout
PLTR stock slipped to a 52-week low of $112.25 on Wednesday amid a broader market rout as investors rotated out of high-growth names and into semiconductor stocks.
The company's shares have also come under pressure as investors weigh mounting regulatory challenges in Europe. Earlier this month, France's domestic intelligence agency replaced Palantir's software with local alternatives, citing a strategy to end reliance on American data and AI software companies to build "digital sovereignty."
Meanwhile, the company is also facing mounting political pressure in the U.K., with British lawmakers pushing to end Palantir's contract with the country's National Health Service.
